PRATIQUE.title: Pratique messages
PRATIQUE.subtitle: International Health Regulations
PRATIQUE.note: By night a red light over a white light may be shown, where it can best be seen, by vessels requiring health clearance. These lights should only be about 6 feet apart, should be exhibited within the precincts of a port and should be visible all around the horizon as nearly as possible.

FLAGS.title: Signaling by flags
FLAGS.subtitle: How a flag signal is made and answered

rows.text: As a general rule only one hoist should be shown at a time. Each hoist is kept flying until the receiving station has answered it. Hoist the signal where the receiving station can see it most easily, with the flags blowing out clear and free from smoke. Groups shown on the same halyard are separated by a tackline.

Hoist the identity signal of the station addressed with the signal. With no identity signal, the signal is addressed to all stations within visual signaling distance. If you do not know the other station’s identity signal, first hoist VF (You should hoist your identity signal) or CS (What is the name or identity signal of your vessel?), together with your own identity signal.

Hoist the answering pennant at the dip as soon as you see each hoist, and close up as soon as you understand it. Lower it to the dip when the hoist is hauled down, and close up again when the next hoist is understood.
After the last hoist, the transmitting station hoists the answering pennant alone to show the signal is complete. The receiving station answers it like any other hoist.

rows.n: When a signal is not understood
rows.text: If you cannot make the signal out, keep the answering pennant at the dip. If you can make it out but not understand it, hoist ZQ (Your signal appears incorrectly coded. You should check and repeat the whole) or ZL (Your signal has been received but not understood).

Substitutes repeat a flag within a group when only one set of flags is carried. The first substitute repeats the uppermost flag of the class (letters or numerals) of the flag just above it; the second repeats the second flag of that class, the third the third. No substitute is used more than once in a group. The answering pennant used as a decimal point is ignored when choosing a substitute. Examples: VV is V, first substitute. 1100 is 1, first substitute, 0, third substitute. L2330 is L, 2, 3, second substitute, 0.
Names in the text of a signal are spelled out with the alphabetical flags. YZ (The words which follow are in plain language) can be used first if necessary.
